summary: Defines a preference header for HTTP requests that expresses a wish to avoid objectionable content. What counts as safe is decided by each origin server and site, and no exact meaning is defined. Support by clients and servers is optional.

eli5.summary: A browser can politely ask a website to keep things family friendly. The website decides what that means, and it does not have to listen.

questions: how to ask a website for safe content
subtitle: A browser can politely ask a website for family-friendly content.

tldr.problem: Many websites offer safe modes to avoid objectionable content, but users must configure this separately on every site and every device, which is cumbersome.
tldr.mechanism: The browser sends a Prefer: safe HTTP header with requests, allowing one configuration to apply across multiple sites. Each origin server decides what 'safe' means for its content.
tldr.outcome: Users can configure their browser or operating system once to request safe content from all sites that support the preference, without requiring accounts or cookies on each site. However, support is optional and the concept of 'safe' is undefined and site-specific.

today: RFC 8674 is an Informational document published independently of the IETF standards track. The safe preference is implemented in some browsers (e.g., Apple's intelligent tracking prevention) but is not universally supported or standardized. Server support varies widely.

sections.title: The Problem of Per-Site Safe Mode Configuration
sections.content:
Many websites offer a 'safe mode' that restricts objectionable content, often through cookies or user accounts. Users who want safe content must individually navigate to each site, create accounts, and set preferences on each one, across every device. This is tedious.

The RFC proposes that the browser itself declare a preference for safe content in HTTP requests, using the HTTP Preference mechanism from RFC 7240. Each server decides how to interpret 'safe' for its own content. Support is optional: servers may ignore the preference, and clients are not required to send it. The expectation is 'best effort,' not a guarantee.
sections.eli5: Instead of going to every website and clicking 'safe mode,' you just tell your browser once, and it asks each website nicely. Some websites will listen, some will not.

sections.title: How the Safe Preference Works
sections.content:
When the browser is configured for safe content, it includes the header Prefer: safe in every HTTPS request (the RFC prohibits it on unencrypted HTTP to prevent intermediaries from injecting or removing it). The server receives this header and may respond with safe content. If the server honors the preference, it should include a Preference-Applied: safe response header to signal that it did so.

What counts as 'objectionable' or 'safe' is entirely up to the origin server. The RFC suggests safe modes often filter content unsuitable for minors, but the definition is subjective and varies by location and cultural context. The server might offer multiple levels of safety through other mechanisms like cookies.

The header must be sent only on HTTPS (encrypted) requests, not on plain HTTP, to avoid interception or tampering by network intermediaries.
sections.eli5: Your browser says 'I would like safe content please' in every request. The website can look at that request and decide to send you the family-friendly version instead of anything else.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Tradeoffs
sections.content:
The safe preference has several security and privacy drawbacks. The header reveals information about the user's preferences, which could be used to fingerprint or profile users by distinguishing them from others. Since the meaning of 'safe' is undefined, different users and servers may have different expectations, leading to inconsistent experiences. Additionally, a malicious server could use the presence of the preference to infer that the user is a minor and target ads or scams accordingly.

Most importantly, the preference does not guarantee safety: malicious servers can ignore it or adapt content to be even worse. The safety of the experience depends entirely on server cooperation. Users who want reliable content filtering should use additional tools like third-party filtering services.

The RFC recommends browsers NOT include the safe preference on unencrypted HTTP, and users in private browsing modes should NOT send it, to avoid leaking the preference to eavesdroppers.
sections.eli5: Sending this preference tells websites something about you, which they could misuse. And a bad website could ignore your request or do something worse. It is like asking politely; it helps, but it is not bulletproof.

sections.title: How Browsers and Sites Can Implement Safe Mode
sections.content:
Browser implementers can add a checkbox to preferences or system settings to enable the safe preference, with clear labeling like 'Request safe content from websites.' Browsers may also allow locking this setting with administrative privileges, so parents can prevent children from disabling it. Administrators or operating systems can set this preference globally.

Server implementers can add support incrementally. Sites that already have safe modes (using cookies or user accounts) can recognize the safe preference and apply their existing safety logic when it arrives. When honoring the preference, if the response changes based on the preference, the server should include Vary: Prefer in the response headers to ensure caches do not serve an unsafe copy to a user who requested safe content.

The RFC recommends servers NOT allow users to disable safe mode through the website's interface if the preference is set by the browser or OS, to prevent circumvention by administrators. However, servers can inform users that safe mode is enabled by a higher-level setting and suggest they contact their administrator.
sections.eli5: Browsers can add one checkbox to enable it globally. Websites that already have safe modes can just look for the header and apply their existing filters.
